citations.citation: John Moses and Joseph Kirkland (eds.), History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 1 (Chicago and New York: Munsell & Co., 1895). Read here for the town before 1836: the immigration chapter 'From Village to City - 1830 to 1837 - the Balloon Age' at printed pages 78-79 and 87-101, the early taverns and hotels at pages 560-561, the 'Real Estate and Insurance' chapter at pages 541-542, the packing trade at page 389, the fire department at pages 207-208, the Kinzie-Clybourn genealogy quoted from Blanchard at page 35, and the Biographical sketches of P. F. W. Peck, Philo Carpenter, John Dean Caton and Alexander N. Fullerton at pages 570-577 and 584; and, for the shore of 1812 (T-0471), the chapter 'The Massacre' at pages 49-50, 54 and 60-61 - the low, discontinuous sand-hills south of Twelfth Street, the scattered cottonwoods on the bank's lower reaches, and the two 'Massacre trees' of Eighteenth Street with Mrs. Kinzie's word that they were saplings in 1812.

transcribes.note: PRINTED AT LENGTH AND NOT MERELY CITED. At pages 34-35 the volume introduces the Kinzie and Clybourn genealogy as 'best told by Rufus Blanchard ... He says:' and sets the whole passage as a block quotation, which is why bk_mose1_019 - Benjamin Hall's 1830 arrival and the town's first tannery - is a reading of Blanchard through Moses and Kirkland and not of Moses and Kirkland. This project does not hold Blanchard and cannot check the transcription. Blanchard in turn credits Benjamin Hall himself for the detail, so the chain to the fact is three deep and the claim says so.
transcribes.work: Rufus Blanchard, Discovery of the Northwest and History of Chicago (Wheaton, Ill.: R. Blanchard & Co., 1881)

what_it_does_not_supply: MOST OF WHAT IT WAS FETCHED FOR. Of the forty-nine lead surnames the Newberry index flagged against this work, thirteen earned a claim, twenty-one appear only outside the pre-1836 window, eight appear early and say nothing usable, one (`black`) is only ever the adjective, four are unresolved because the volume carries a surname one character from the index card's spelling, and two are absent outright. The full row-by-row result is committed at data/research/books/moses_kirkland_v1_lead_surnames.json so the next run does not pay for the search twice.

VOLUME 2, WHICH IS HALF THE WORK. Only volume 1 is read. The Newberry cards do not say which volume they cite, so an absence recorded here may simply be in the other book, and every ABSENT verdict in the lookup file says so on itself.

AN INDEPENDENT VOICE. It is a compilation of 1895 and it names its own authorities on the pages read: Andreas for Garrett's $1,800,000 of auction sales, Bross's History of Chicago page 38 for the earliest deeds, the Story of Chicago page 130 for Caton's election tally, Hurlbut's Chicago Antiquities pages 37-8 for the pre-1830 settler list, S. R. Beggs's West and Northwest page 95 for the Black Hawk alarm, and Rufus Blanchard's Discovery of the Northwest and History of Chicago (1881) quoted at length for the Kinzie-Clybourn genealogy. Where the sentence itself credits another work, the claim says so and the citation must go to that work and not to this one.
A SINGLE ADDRESS IN THE MODERN SENSE, and no street numbers. Positions here are corners, lots, blocks, a river bank and a tree.

ANY DATE FINER THAN THE YEAR for two things this project wanted finer: Caton's marriage, which is given as '1835' with the scene date sitting in the middle of it, and the Hubbard-Marsh packing partnership, which is 'later'.

CONSISTENCY WITH ITSELF. Page 89 dates Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings to 1832 while page 570 has Peck's occupied in the fall of 1831; page 207 forms the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company on 7 October 1835 while page 570 has it organised on 20 October 1835. Both readings of each are recorded and neither is adopted.
what_it_supplies: A TRADE CENSUS OF THE WHOLE TOWN, at page 95: the State census taken between 1 September and December 1835 counted 3,297 people, forty-four stores, two book stores, four druggists, two silversmiths and jewellers, two tin and copper manufactories, two printing offices, two breweries, one steam saw-mill, one iron foundry, four storage and forwarding houses, eight taverns, one lottery office, one bank, five churches, seven schools, twenty-two lawyers, fourteen physicians, and a lyceum and reading room. The project had no denominator for its business layer and this is one - for December 1835 and not for July.

A BUILDING WITH FOUR OF THE FIVE FIELDS data/structures/ WANTS, at page 90: John S. C. Hogan's story-and-a-half log storehouse, 45 by 18 feet, at the angle where Lake and South Water streets meet, with the post office partitioned off inside it from 2 November 1832.

TWO RESIDENCES STATED AS SUCH, which is the field the town is thinnest in: Rev. Jeremiah Porter lodging and keeping his study in the second storey of Peck's store from May 1833 (page 571), and John Dean Caton renting the back room and attic of Dr Temple's Temple Building from December 1833, sleeping in the attic and practising law in the back room, and sub-letting desk-room in it to his competitor Spring (page 577).

BUSINESSES GIVEN BY CORNER, LOT OR LANDMARK: Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings at the south-east corners of South Water and Dearborn and of South Water and La Salle (page 89); Peck's two-storey frame store of black walnut brought from Detroit, occupied in the fall of 1831 (page 570); Sylvester Marsh killing beef under an old elm on the open prairie at what became Monroe Street from the winter of 1833-4 (page 389); William Jones's lots 2 and 7 in block 17 fronting Water and Lake (page 542).

OCCUPATIONS AND ARRIVALS for men this project already holds: Philo Carpenter as the town's first druggist, arriving within a month before 19 August 1832; Benjamin Hall as proprietor of the first tannery ever established there, arriving 1830; Dole, Clybourn, the Noble brothers and Gurdon S. Hubbard beginning the slaughtering and packing trade in 1832; the 1833 spring arrivals including Caton, Kimball and Asahel Pierce; and Hubbard's permanent residence dated to 1832 by the compiler's own reason for leaving him off a list.

TWO PRESENCE LISTS: the twenty-two men who signed the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company roll on 7 October 1835 (pages 207-208), and, unread and left for its own ticket, the 'LIST OF ACTUAL SETTLERS AT CHICAGO, PRIOR TO 1830' at pages 78-79, about thirty rows with nativity, year and remarks columns.
ONE STATEMENT ABOUT THE GROUND OF THE SCENE, at page 79: the winter of 1834-5 was open, with little snow, front doors standing open all winter, and cattle living on grass on the river bank.

endings.text: Nails to drive and brick for a chimney: the list is short and complete. The Lake House will want a great deal more of both.
Nail rods for a smith and brick for a chimney: the list is done, and some of the work is still to be hammered out.
Ironwork for the shingles and no brick this season: a plain roof first, and the chimney another year. It will stand the first high wind.

evidence.locator: 1 July 1835, p. 4, col. 4, the card headed 'NEWBERRY & [DOLE,] Storage, Forwarding and C[ommission] MERCHAN[TS]' (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1835_07_01#c015). Transcription-mediated reading; the brackets are the transcription's.
evidence.text: In the Chicago Democrat of 1 July 1835, Newberry & Dole advertise as storage, forwarding and commission merchants and agents for the Merchants' Line, and also as wholesale and retail dealers in dry goods, groceries and provisions.

evidence.reasoning: The trade style is the firm's own and the June 1834 Peck notice says his stock came from New York. That builders' ironwork in particular came through a forwarding house such as this one is read from the trade name and from where Peck's stock came from, not from any record of a consignment, so the stop claims the kind of business and no shipment.
evidence.text: A forwarding and commission house received goods landed from vessels and sent them on to, or sold them for, other traders; manufactured goods such as iron reached the town that way, as Peck's own notice of stock just received from New York shows.

evidence.reasoning: Follows the structure record newberry_dole_warehouse, whose position is reconstructed and whose note carries both readings without settling them. The stop says the bank is disputed and claims no front door.
evidence.text: Where Newberry & Dole's warehouse stood is disputed: one dossier reads the south bank on South Water Street, Andreas puts the firm's warehouse on the north bank east of the later Rush Street bridge. The scene places it on the south bank as a reconstruction, so the stop claims the firm, not the spot.

evidence.locator: 2 July 1834, p. 4, col. 4, the card headed 'New Goods! New Goods!', dated June 18, 1834 (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1834_07_02#c023). Transcription-mediated reading.
evidence.text: P. F. W. Peck, at the corner of LaSalle and South Water streets, advertises that he has just received from New York a full stock of fresh goods, which he offers at very low prices for cash or country produce.

evidence.locator: 10 Sept 1834, p. 3, col. 1 (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1834_09_10#c005); the same notice printed 17 Sept 1834, p. 3, col. 3. Transcription-mediated reading of a damaged line; the notice gives no address.
evidence.text: A notice signed P. F. W. Peck offers nails, English blister and cast steel, nail rods and assorted bar iron for sale.

evidence.reasoning: Andreas and Peck's own cards name the corner. The structure record peck_store derives the coordinate from the modern intersection and grades it inferred; the stop claims the corner, and claims no interior and no clerk.
evidence.text: Peck's store stood at the south-west corner of South Water and LaSalle streets; the corner is attested and the coordinate is derived from it.

evidence.reasoning: The September 1834 notice lists nails and nail rods as separate lines of the same stock. What a nail rod was for is read from the ordinary meaning of the trade term; that it was cheaper and slower is the general shape of buying stock rather than the finished article, not a price anyone in Chicago recorded.
evidence.text: Nail rods are iron rod stock from which a smith cut and headed nails by hand; offered beside ready nails, they are the cheaper and slower way to the same roof.

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, scan p. 1161, the brick-making paragraph beginning 'In the spring of 1833, Tyler K. Blodgett established a brick-yard'.
evidence.text: Andreas: in the spring of 1833 Tyler K. Blodgett established a brick-yard on the North Side, not far from the river bank, between Dearborn and Clark streets, and engaged Henry S. Lampman, then of Ann Arbor, as a workman; Lampman was undoubtedly the first brick-maker.

evidence.reasoning: Follows the structure record brickyard_north_side, which grades the position inferred from Andreas's locating sentence. The yard is an area and the scene draws one drying shed for it; the clamp, pit and hacks are recorded and not built, as the stop says.
evidence.text: The yard's shed is placed midway between the lines of Clark and Dearborn streets, about 17 m back from the traced north bank; the sentence bounds the block and the spot within it is the record's choice.

evidence.reasoning: The structure record carries the yard's range to 1835 as inference from the town's brick building and says whether Blodgett was still on this ground is not attested; the stop says who worked it in July 1835 is not recorded, and does not say the Lake House's brick came from here.
evidence.text: That the yard was still worked on 1 July 1835 is inference: the Lake House going up in brick on the same bank is the best reason to think somebody was making brick in the town, and nothing says who.

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, the hotels paragraph beginning 'Chicago did, however, have a really grand hotel as early as 1835', as transcribed under the heading 'Andreas' History of Chicago Volume I' on chicagology prefire112 (accessed 2026-08-11).
evidence.text: Andreas: Chicago had a really grand hotel as early as 1835, the Lake House, at the corners of Kinzie, Rush and Michigan streets, fronting on the latter; built of brick, three stories and a basement in height; completed and thrown open to the public in the autumn of 1836.

evidence.locator: Chicagology prefire112, the uncredited paragraph beginning 'The Lake House hotel on the north side of the river', immediately after the Andreas paragraph (accessed 2026-08-11).
evidence.text: An uncredited modern paragraph says ground was broken for the Lake House in 1835; Andreas gives no groundbreaking, and this project grades the paragraph as its weakest kind of source.

evidence.locator: p. 94-95, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12761-12791 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)
evidence.text: In 1834 the old frame of heavy sills, posts and beams 'was found too slow', and 'the balloon frame, originated by George W. Snow' came in: timbers 'a foot square' gave place to ones 'two by four inches', and despite 'the prediction that they would be blown away by the first high wind', they 'were found sufficiently strong to weather the gale and the storm'.

evidence.locator: p. 90, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12240-12258 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)
evidence.text: In 1833 about 165 frame buildings went up, and one of brick, 'the first in the town outside the fort', built by Alanson Sweet and William Worthingham for John Noble on a lot next to the one the Lake House later took.

evidence.locator: p. 561, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 98826-98837 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)
evidence.text: Before the Lake House was finished, the first Unitarian service in Chicago was held in it, conducted by the Rev. Dr. Follen, with Harriet Martineau in the congregation; the inn 'aimed to cater for only the highest class of guests'.

evidence.reasoning: Follows the structure record lake_house_construction and its liberty: a building finished in autumn 1836 and begun, on the compilations, in 1835 is a building site on the scene date, and the record reasons one storey from the build schedule and grades it conjectural. The stop calls the shell our reconstruction and offers an exterior look only.
evidence.text: On 1 July 1835 the scene draws the Lake House as a roofless brick shell one storey high, on the east side of Rush Street; the storey count, the plan and the side of the street are not documented.

The builder, the small frame house and its roof, the list, the choice of nails or nail rods, the choice of brick or none, the route, the endings, the timing inputs and the Builder's List keepsake are invented connective narrative. No order, price, sale or customer of any firm is documented, and no named person is met.

keepsake.text: A fictional list of what one small roof wanted in July 1835. No real order, price or sale by any merchant or brickmaker is written on it.

opening.text:
JAUNT: MATERIALS FOR A ROOF. You are putting up a small frame house, and you are doing it the new Chicago way. The old frame of heavy beams 'was found too slow', so the town builds with 'the balloon frame, originated by George W. Snow': light timbers 'two by four inches', nailed fast. People predicted these houses would 'be blown away by the first high wind'. They were wrong.

The roof is next. See what comes in by lake, choose the ironwork at Peck's corner, look in at the first brickyard, and end at the Lake House, the grandest building in town, still going up.

premise: Draw up a builder's list for one small roof: what comes by lake at Newberry & Dole's, nails or nail rods at Peck's corner, brick or none at the town's first brickyard, and a look at the Lake House site.

stops.narrative: What the town cannot make, the lake brings.
stops.text: Start at Newberry & Dole's warehouse on the river. In the Democrat of 1 July 1835 they advertise storage, forwarding and commission, agents for the Merchants' Line. A balloon frame needs nails by the keg, and nails, glass and iron do not grow on the prairie: what the town cannot make comes in by lake and lands at houses like this one.

choices.label: A keg of nails, ready to drive

choices.consequence: Rods go on the list, and a smith's work after them.
choices.label: Nail rods, for a smith to head

stops.narrative: Settle the ironwork before the brick.
stops.text: Along South Water Street to Peck's corner at LaSalle. In September 1834 he advertised nails, nail rods, bar iron and English blister and cast steel, his stock 'just received from New York'. A roof wants nails, and a balloon frame wants a great many more. Choose how to buy them.

choices.consequence: The chimney can wait for another summer.
choices.label: No brick this season

stops.narrative: Brick or none, and the list is done.
stops.text: Over the river to the North Side, where Andreas puts Tyler K. Blodgett's brickyard of spring 1833 near the bank, with Henry S. Lampman, 'undoubtedly the first brick-maker'. The first brick building outside the fort went up that same year, for John Noble, on the lot next to where the Lake House is rising. In a town of 165 new frames, one brick house was news. One shed stands for the yard.

stops.narrative: Whose brick goes into it, nobody wrote down.
stops.text: East along the bank to Rush Street and the Lake House. Andreas describes the finished hotel: brick, three storeys and a basement, opened in autumn 1836, and it 'aimed to cater for only the highest class of guests'. Before it was even finished, the first Unitarian service in Chicago was held inside, with the English writer Harriet Martineau in the congregation. Look from the street at the walls going up.
